title: How To Deal With Your Students' Sagging Pants
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that sagging pants, though seemingly trivial, correlate with an attitude of rebelliousness that undermines respect for rules and learning. Rather than confronting the behavior personally, he advises teachers to point to an existing school dress code policy, or create their own classroom policy if none exists, and lay it out clearly during first-days-of-school lessons alongside consequences. The key mechanism is that policies announced and taught ahead of time feel fair to students, while rules introduced reactively in the moment feel arbitrary and personal. He describes enforcing the dress code as simply invoking a pre-taught consequence, not a confrontation. He closes by describing the broader payoff: students who understand a clear, non-negotiable dress standard feel safer, more disciplined, and more respected, even the most challenging students who may not respect other adults in their lives.
points: Sagging pants correlate with an attitude of rebelliousness and antagonism toward rules, distinct from style or culture.
Rather than confronting students personally, teachers should point to an existing dress code or create and teach their own.
Policies explained ahead of time during first-days-of-school lessons feel fair; rules introduced reactively feel arbitrary and personal.
Enforcing a pre-taught dress code is simply invoking a known consequence, removing the discomfort of the confrontation.
Consistent, non-negotiable standards that protect students are respected even by the most challenging students.
quotes: Sagging pants are a problem in the classroom. They’re a problem because they bring an attitude of rebelliousness.
All fine and good. But it’s linked with disrespect. It’s linked with antagonism toward rules, authority, listening, and learning.
Part of being a leader is doing what is right for your students even if they or others disagree.
If you lay it out the first of the year, if you let your students know up front what is expected, then they’ll accept it. Grudgingly perhaps, but they understand.
A teacher who requires non-negotiable standards that are best for students is respected. They’re respected even by the most challenging students who may not respect another adult in their life.
It’s a simple little thing, sagging pants, but like all details, when added up, make a big difference.
